finding: §1 was rewritten this round to "One deliverable, and it is behaviour-preserving by default. §2 ships audit_converge_on -- its resolution, its fence, its validation and its documentation". §4 Non-Goal 6 then puts a fifth thing in scope, in bold: "The breakdown is in scope and ships on --merge", a by_severity counter over non-PASS rows in audit_merge.go's existing loop (verified: the loop is at :61-76 and the compact-stripped key at :90-92, so the citation is sound). That deliverable is not resolution, fence, validation or documentation; it is a new output key on a third command, it appears nowhere in §2, and §5 has no test for it -- while §5's closing "What is not tested here, named so its absence is deliberate" names only role_streaks[].open and spec_coverage_clean_rounds. So the release's only statement of scope (§1) and its list of tests (§5) both exclude a deliverable that a section headed Non-Goals declares in scope. An implementer decomposing from §1 and §2 will not build it; one decomposing from §4 will build it untested and unmentioned in the Overview.
suggestion: Pick one. Either move the by_severity breakdown into §2 as a named deliverable, correct §1's "One deliverable" to say what the second is, and add a §5 test with its killing mutation (a merge that counts PASS rows' null severity into the breakdown); or leave it out of the release entirely and let Non-Goal 6 defer the breakdown with the count, as the rest of the paragraph already does. A Non-Goal is not a place to add scope.

finding: §2.2's load-bearing paragraph asserts an architecture the twin it copies does not have. It says: 'ReviewRound.Clean is stamped at record time, so a round recorded in 2026 is never re-graded under a knob set later: those 67 rows are read by no predicate this release adds.' That is true of TODAY's audit path (audit_record.go:71 stamps clean := findings == 0 and engine.Converged -> ConsecutiveClean reads the stamped flag), but §2 says four times that this release is the twin of review_converge_on, and the twin does the opposite: ReviewConsecutiveClean (engine/reviewclean.go:119-128) re-grades EVERY recorded round live via ReviewRoundClean(specPath, &rounds[i], convergeOn), and engine/reviewclean.go:91-93 states the choice as a design intent -- 'Read live from the round's recorded findings ... so a later --resolve or converge-on switch re-evaluates it without re-recording'. If the audit side is built as the twin, the 67 legacy rows in 15 files ARE read by the predicate this release adds, §2's fail-closed rule makes all 15 historical round files blocking, and every converged pre-v0.33.0 cycle flips to not-converged on install -- the exact retroactivity §3 cut the release's second deliverable for. §2.2's numbers all verify (67 = high 16 / medium 15 / low 36 across 15 files; 238 non-PASS and 0 out-of-enum across v0.33.0-v0.36.0; 2,913 PASS rows all severity null); only its premise does not.
suggestion: §2 must state whether audit_converge_on is evaluated at record time or live per round, and §2.2 must then be rewritten to whichever it is. If record-time: say so explicitly and say that this DIVERGES from review_converge_on, and drop 'this is its twin'. If live: §2.2's dismissal of the 67 rows is false and the retroactive-blocking outcome needs the same decision §3 deferred to spec/0.46.0.md §8.4.

finding: The reversed-guard count moved from one to two this round and is still short by the one that matters most, because the third is not a test literal but a shipped code constant on the agent-facing JSON contract. engine.DivergenceHint (internal/engine/divergence.go:16-19) ends '...; audit convergence still counts every non-PASS row.' — the same clause §4's second guard names in SKILL.md, but here it is a const emitted verbatim as divergence.hint on tp audit --status and tp audit --record. Under blocking the clause is false, and it is false in exactly the situation the object is emitted for: divergence fires when spec-coverage is clean while other roles hold open findings, which is the population blocking exists to stop counting. So an operator who sets blocking is told by tp's own payload that the knob they set does not exist. The constant is pinned in five further places §4 names none of: docs_contract_test.go:145 (assert.Contains(reference, engine.DivergenceHint) — REFERENCE.md:876-880 quotes it in a fenced block), divergence_test.go:166 and :176 (the JSONEq shape), audit_signal_test.go:101, :128 and :303. §4 says 'named as claims rather than as filenames, since an earlier draft scoped the docs by file and the two sentences this release actually falsifies went unnamed for two rounds' — the same defect has now recurred one layer down: a claim, not a file, and it lives in code.
suggestion: Name it as the third reversal and state what it costs: the constant's last clause becomes severity-aware wording true under both values (e.g. '...; audit convergence counts every non-PASS row unless audit_converge_on is blocking'), REFERENCE.md:879's fenced quote moves with it byte-for-byte because docs_contract_test.go:145 compares the document against the constant, and divergence_test.go's JSONEq plus the three audit_signal_test.go assertions read the constant symbolically and need no edit. Add a §5 test asserting the emitted divergence.hint no longer states the unconditional rule; killing input is the shipped constant left unchanged. Alternatively decide the constant is out of scope and say so — but then §4 must stop claiming a count, because 'two guards' is falsified by the same evidence that falsified 'one'.

finding: The second-guard paragraph says "This release updates both, and §5 test 3's doc assertions are over that sentence and SKILL.md:145's --status --check clause". §5 test 3 is "The two surfaces v0.31.1 exists for" -- tp config --extract and tp validate --project -- and carries no doc assertion at all. Reading §5 end to end, none of the eleven tests asserts anything about SKILL.md or REFERENCE.md, and none pins the reversal of the second shipped guard docs_contract_test.go:96 (verified: divergenceCountingSubstring = "audit convergence still counts every non-PASS row", pinning SKILL.md:149). So §1 lists documentation as one of the four things this release ships, §4 names a shipped guard that must be reversed to ship it, and §5 tests neither -- while pointing at a test number that is about something else. The doc deliverable is the one part of the release with a red-then-green guard already in the tree and no test claiming it.
suggestion: Add a §5 test: after the release, SKILL.md no longer contains "audit convergence still counts every non-PASS row" and docs_contract_test.go's replacement literal is the sentence that is true under both values; killing mutation = shipping the field while leaving SKILL.md unedited, which must redden that test. Then repoint §4's cross-reference at the new test number, or delete the "§5 test 3's doc assertions" clause.

finding: §4 says the two doc sentences this release falsifies are "named as claims rather than as filenames, since an earlier draft scoped the docs by file and the two sentences this release actually falsifies went unnamed for two rounds" -- and then names one sentence that is NOT falsified and misses the one that is. SKILL.md:145 reads "A disposition is not an escape hatch from the gate: tp audit --record counts every row whose status is not exactly PASS and reads no disposition at all, so parking a finding leaves the round's finding count, the role streak and --status --check exactly where they were." Under blocking that whole sentence still holds: §2 states blocking governs clean and nothing else, countAuditFindings is untouched, a disposition still changes nothing, and Non-Goal 2 keeps it true on purpose. The sentence blocking does falsify is SKILL.md:144 -- "a row counts as a finding when status is absent or != PASS; a clean round has zero findings" -- whose second clause is exactly what the release inverts, and §4 never names it. Nothing pins SKILL.md:144, so unlike the :149 sentence it reddens no test when it goes stale.
suggestion: Replace the SKILL.md:145 citation with SKILL.md:144's "a clean round has zero findings", and state its counterpart under blocking (a clean round has zero BLOCKING findings). If the :145 clause is meant to stay, say explicitly that it survives unchanged rather than listing it among the falsified claims.

finding: §4's closing paragraph delegates the SECOND deliberately reversed guard to a test that does not contain it. It says of internal/cli/docs_contract_test.go:96 -- which pins the literal 'audit convergence still counts every non-PASS row' in SKILL.md -- 'This release updates both, and §5 test 3's doc assertions are over that sentence and SKILL.md:145's --status --check clause'. §5 test 3 has no doc assertion: it reads in full 'The two surfaces v0.31.1 exists for. tp config --extract emits the field and tp validate --project accepts and rejects it'. So the release names two sentences it falsifies, names the shipped guard that reddens, and then routes the acceptance to a test about a different subject. The consequence is the hazard §4 itself raises one paragraph earlier for the FIRST guard: an implementer with spec cover for 'reversing the guard' can satisfy the suite by DELETING docs_contract_test.go:96 rather than updating its literal, and no test in §5 distinguishes the two outcomes. §4 protects the first guard by naming three of its nine surviving assertions; the second guard gets no such protection.
suggestion: Either add a §5 test 12 pinning the two replacement literals (the new SKILL.md sentence and the new SKILL.md:145 --status --check clause) and asserting docs_contract_test.go still contains a doc-contract assertion over each, or extend test 3 to actually carry them and say so in its text. Do not leave §4 pointing at test 3 for assertions test 3 does not make.

finding: 019c31e rewrote §1 to read "One deliverable, and it is behaviour-preserving by default ... changes nothing for a project that does not set it" and, in the same commit, rewrote Non-Goal 6 to read "The breakdown is in scope and ships on --merge" — a new by_severity key emitted by tp audit --merge for every project, whether or not audit_converge_on is set. That is a second deliverable and it is not behaviour-preserving by default, which is the exact sentence shape §1 had just been repaired for removing ("§3 changes consecutive_clean and converged for any project whose spec moves between rounds, opted in or not"). The repair fixed the paragraph and reintroduced the condition that made it wrong.
suggestion: Pick one. Either keep the release single-deliverable and return the --merge by_severity breakdown to spec/0.46.0.md §8.3 (which already says the breakdown is 0.37.0's, so both files move together), or restate §1 as "two deliverables: audit_converge_on, which is opt-in, and a by_severity breakdown on tp audit --merge, which is unconditional" and drop the "changes nothing" clause.

finding: 019c31e added "`spec/0.31.0.md:41` and `spec/0.35.0.md:568-573` keep their copies: those are shipped specs and `spec/0.34.0.md` Non-Goal 6 forbids editing one." The 0.35.0 half is false and the paragraph contradicts itself two sentences later. Read: spec/0.35.0.md:568-573 is the CORRECTED three-layer statement ("which for workflow fields is task override > project config > built-in ... Two exceptions: notify_cmd ... and TP_RUNNER_SEAM"). The five-layer copy in that file is at :575 alone, and only as a record of an earlier draft. The next sentence of §2 then calls the same range "the most accurate text in the repository on this point" — so one paragraph says :568-573 both carries the error Non-Goal 6 forbids fixing and is the most accurate text there is. Round 5's own commit a6d80f1 got this right in its message: "spec/0.35.0.md:575 keeps its copy: that one is the historical record of the removal." The repair replaced a correct pointer with a wrong one.
suggestion: Cite spec/0.35.0.md:575, not :568-573, as the surviving copy — and say it is the historical record of the removal rather than an uncorrected error, since Non-Goal 6 is not why it stands. Keep the separate reference to §7/:568-573 as the accurate statement.

finding: The replaced fence paragraph asserts and then denies the same fact eleven lines apart. It opens "the only workflow-write fence is fenceWorkflowWrite(field string, requested float64) in internal/cli/unattended.go:56 -- numeric by signature, covering caps and command fields", then states "The mechanism already exists and is not the numeric one" and names a second workflow-write fence that ships today at set.go:361-362 and set_project.go:46-47. Both cannot be true, and the false half is the one a top-down reader reaches first. The subordinate claim "covering caps and command fields" is also wrong about what runs: fenceWorkflowWrite does test FencedCommandField at unattended.go:60, but that branch is unreachable from all four cited call sites -- runner and notify_cmd are in neither floatWorkflowFields nor editableWorkflowFields, and set.go:361 / set_project.go:46 already refuse them before the type dispatch -- so the function covers caps and nothing else in practice. A third site carries the same string guard, set_local.go:41, which the paragraph does not mention.
suggestion: Rewrite the opening clause to what the code shows: tp has two workflow-write fences, a numeric one keyed on FencedCapField (four call sites, all after ParseFloat/Atoi) and a string one keyed on FencedCommandField (three call sites, all before the type dispatch: set.go:361, set_project.go:46, set_local.go:41), and this release extends the second. Drop "covering caps and command fields", or say the command branch is unreachable from the numeric call sites.

finding: §2 prescribes the fence as a verbatim copy of a shipping guard: the code block is `if engine.Unattended() && engine.FencedCommandField(field) { refuseUnattendedCommandField(field)`, and the instruction is "a third predicate beside FencedCapField and FencedCommandField, and that guard copied at both sites". Copying that guard shape means calling refuseUnattendedCommandField, whose message is fixed at unattended.go:46: "%s names a command the driver executes and cannot be set under TP_UNATTENDED, at any layer". Both halves are false of audit_converge_on -- it names no command, and it does not resolve at any layer (§2 itself says the precedence is task override > project config > built-in, with no local layer, whereas "at any layer" was written for notify_cmd, whose only layer is .tp/local.json). The refusal a unit reads is the whole product of this fence, and §5 test 9 pins exit 2 and exit 0 only, so an implementation that emits the command-field message passes every test in §5 while telling the operator something untrue about the field they set.
suggestion: Say in §2 that the third predicate needs its own refusal, not refuseUnattendedCommandField -- a message naming audit_converge_on as a gate-relaxing field refused in both directions -- and give §5 test 9 an assertion over the refusal text and over --decision audit-converge-on (test 10 already needs the second half), so the wrong-message implementation has a failing arm.

finding: §2 says "the enum's cardinality is asserted in nine places that must move with it, counted" and lists escalation.go:14,29,39,47; escalation_test.go:60; cli/escalate_test.go:158; fakerunner/.../main.go:260; REFERENCE.md:347; SKILL.md:247. I checked each (all nine are real) and then swept the tree for the five-literal enumeration. Two sites are missing, and one of them is cited by the very sentence that makes the count: (1) internal/cli/escalate.go:41 -- the command's own --help text, "--decision is one of skip-gate, raise-review-cap, raise-audit-cap, import-force or other" -- which §2 names three lines earlier as where the enum lives, and which is user-facing output that is simply wrong the moment a sixth value ships; (2) skills/tp/SKILL.md:372, "tp escalate --decision <skip-gate|raise-review-cap|raise-audit-cap|import-force|other>", a full five-literal enumeration in the Gate/Budget/Escalation policy section. Eleven, not nine. This is the exhaustiveness-claim class CLAUDE.md records five rounds of v0.36.0's audit falsifying, and here the omitted site is the one the same sentence cites.
suggestion: Either raise the count to eleven and add escalate.go:41 and SKILL.md:372 to the list, or -- better, per the same rule -- bind the claim to an artifact instead of a number: state the invariant ("no five-literal enumeration of the decision set survives the release") and make it a guard test or a workflow.checks entry that greps for the four non-`other` literals appearing together, so the list cannot go stale silently.

finding: §2 says 'Both write paths are fenced' and names tp set --workflow and its --project form. There is a third supported path to the same task-override layer and it is open under TP_UNATTENDED: tp import. importcmd.go:36-42 fences only --force; a full-TaskFile import writes tf.Workflow straight from the document (importcmd.go:90-93, and the preservation branch at :158-161 only carries the OLD block over when the imported document has no workflow key), so `TP_UNATTENDED=1 tp import tasks.json` with {"workflow":{"audit_converge_on":"blocking"}} exits 0 and persists the relaxing value the fence exists to refuse. §5 test 9 cannot see this: it drives the two set commands only. Two honest qualifications, because the claim should be judged on what is new here. First, the same route already bypasses the cap fence for review_max_rounds, so the hole is a class tp already has rather than one this release invents. Second, that is exactly why it matters now: §2 argues audit_converge_on is 'the first string-valued workflow field whose non-default value relaxes a gate' and that 'the fence is not a detail of this release — it is what the release buys'. A fence a unit walks around by importing is worth less than the section claims, and 'both write paths' is a two-over-an-unenumerated-set claim of the shape CLAUDE.md records five rounds of v0.36.0 falsifying.
suggestion: Either fence it — refuse an imported workflow block carrying audit_converge_on under TP_UNATTENDED, with a third §5 arm whose killing input is a plain (non---force) import of such a document — or scope the claim honestly: 'The two tp set paths are fenced. tp import writes the same layer and is not fenced for any workflow field; closing that is <spec>, not this release.' The first costs one guard at importcmd.go beside the existing --force check; the second costs a sentence and stops §2 asserting a coverage it does not have.

finding: §2 scopes the enum change to the nine (really eleven) sites that state the decision set's cardinality, and stops there. But adding audit-converge-on does not only grow an enum -- it creates a fifth user-only decision, and tp's agent-facing documents close that set at four in prose the enum sweep does not touch: SKILL.md:185 "the four user-only decisions fail closed with exit 2" followed by its three-item enumeration; SKILL.md:372 "the four decisions above"; CLAUDE.md:180 "the four user-approved decisions this file has always reserved for the operator" and CLAUDE.md:89's three-item list; escalate.go:32's "(--skip-gate, raising a review or audit cap, tp import --force)". All become false on the day the fence ships. Worse for SKILL.md:185 specifically: it states a two-category fence taxonomy -- caps refused only on a raise, runner/notify_cmd refused "at every layer" -- and §2's "The fence is on the field, not on the direction" introduces a third category that fits neither. §1 lists documentation as a deliverable but §2's documentation scope is the enum sites only, so the decision-count prose and the taxonomy are in nobody's acceptance.
suggestion: Add to §2's scope: the four-decisions prose in SKILL.md and CLAUDE.md becomes five, and SKILL.md:185's fence taxonomy gains a third row (a field fenced in both directions at both workflow write layers, refused for naming no command but relaxing a gate). Name the claims rather than the files, as §4's second-guard paragraph already tries to do.

finding: §2's repaired sentence 'the enum's cardinality is asserted in nine places that must move with it, counted' is miscounted in both directions, measured against the tree. Of the nine listed, engine/escalation.go:29 asserts NO cardinality -- it reads '// escalationDecisions is the closed set in the order §5.2 writes it, which is' and names no number. The 'not a sixth category' comment §2 quotes as being among 14,29,39,47 is at :19-20, not :29. Three sites that DO assert the cardinality are missing from the list: engine/escalation.go:19 ('not a sixth category'), internal/cli/escalate_test.go:154 ('pins §5.2's closed set') and internal/cli/escalate_test.go:157 -- the function NAME TestEscalateAcceptsTheFiveDecisions. A repo-wide scan for /[Ff]ive|sixth/ within four lines of decision|escalat|skip-gate|import-force returns eleven such sites, not nine (the eight correct listed ones plus those three; escalate_test.go:72's 'five variables' is about env vars and is correctly excluded). Worse for testability: none of the eleven goes red on a sixth entry. TestEscalateAcceptsTheFiveDecisions loops the five string literals and asserts each is ACCEPTED (escalate_test.go:158-168), so it passes unchanged once a sixth exists, leaving a test function whose name says five while the enum holds six. §5 test 10 pins only that a refusal names audit-converge-on, so nothing in the release's acceptance detects the drift.
suggestion: Re-derive the list against the tree (drop :29, add :19, :154 and :157, say eleven), or -- better, per this repo's own rule that a claim a guard enforces cannot drift -- replace the prose count with a guard: assert len(engine.EscalationDecisions()) == 6 in engine/escalation_test.go and add that assertion to §5 test 10, so a seventh entry cannot land without the count moving.

finding: Non-Goal 6 now puts a deliverable in scope — 'The breakdown is in scope and ships on --merge ... a by_severity counter over non-PASS rows' — and it arrives with no test, no field shape, and no home in the release's own description. Three concrete gaps an implementer cannot close by reading. (1) §5 has eleven tests and none touches --merge; §5's closing paragraph claims to enumerate what is deliberately untested and names only role_streaks and spec_coverage_clean_rounds, so by_severity is untested and unlisted, and an implementation that ships without it passes every test in the release. (2) The key set is unspecified. §2's fail-closed rule is stated for the clean PREDICATE, not for a counter, so it does not answer what by_severity does with a row whose severity is null (2,913 PASS rows carry exactly that per §2, though those are excluded here), absent, or out of enum — count it under a synthetic key, under 'error' by the fail-closed analogy, or drop it, which would make the counter's total silently disagree with the summary's own findings count. §2.2's 67 legacy rows guarantee high/medium/low appear in real inputs. (3) --compact is unstated. Non-Goal 6's own citation is ':90-92 already carries a --compact-stripped explanatory key', which reads as an argument that by_severity is stripped too, while REFERENCE.md:641's rule is that decision-critical fields survive and explanatory ones do not — and a breakdown an operator needs to see what blocking suppressed is decision-critical by that rule. Also: §1 still says 'One deliverable', and this is a second one, located inside a Non-Goals section rather than in §2.
suggestion: Move the by_severity paragraph out of Non-Goal 6 into §2 (or its own §2.3) so a deliverable is not specified inside a list of things the release does not do, and pin the three open points: 'by_severity counts non-PASS rows by their severity string; a row whose severity is absent, null or out of enum is counted under the key "unknown"; the counter's values sum to findings; it survives --compact because it is what an operator setting blocking reads to see what was suppressed.' Add a §5 test over a merge input mixing error/warning/info with one out-of-enum and one absent-severity row, killing input a merge that emits by_status and by_role without by_severity. Then fix §1 to say two deliverables, or fold the counter into §2 and keep the count at one.

finding: Round 6's `by_severity` argument was taken, and the deliverable it created lives entirely inside a list item titled "An audit-side `nonblocking_open` on `--record` and `--status`" in a section titled Non-Goals. Counted against the file: the strings `--merge`, `by_severity` and `audit_merge` occur on lines 230-234 and nowhere else in 312 lines -- all four occurrences inside Non-Goal 6. Every other surface that decides what gets built disagrees with it. §1 sizes the release as "**One deliverable**" and enumerates §2's four parts ("its resolution, its fence, its validation and its documentation") -- no output key. §2, the section an implementer reads for scope, never names `--merge`. §5's eleven tests never name it, so the one new emitted key in the release has no failing arm; §5's closing paragraph, which exists to name untested things deliberately, says "`clean` is this release's only gated surface" and lists `role_streaks[].open` and `spec_coverage_clean_rounds` -- a new JSON key on `--merge` is neither tested nor named as untested. The AX consequence is specific rather than stylistic: a decomposer builds §5's tests and §2's scope, and Non-Goals is the list it reads to learn what NOT to build, so the key does not ship, `clean: true` under `blocking` stays unreadable, and Non-Goal 6's own closing sentence -- "an operator setting `blocking` reads the round files for what was suppressed" -- survives as the shipped behaviour while the paragraph above it says the fix is in scope. The item also asserts both halves at once: its bolded title defers the thing and its bolded body says "The breakdown is in scope and ships on `--merge`".
suggestion: Move the two scope sentences out of Non-Goal 6 into §2 as a named part of the deliverable -- `tp audit --merge`'s summary gains `by_severity`, a count of non-`PASS` rows by severity including §2's unrecognised bucket, emitted only when a non-`PASS` row exists and omitted under `--compact` like `overlap_report` (`audit_merge.go:90-92`) -- and update §1's enumeration to five parts. Add a §5 test whose killing mutation is named (a counter that includes `PASS` rows, or one that survives `--compact`). Retitle Non-Goal 6 to what it now defers -- the `--record`/`--status` counterpart and its four pins -- so the section title and the item title agree.

finding: The doc repair this round names the claims correctly and then points their acceptance at a test that contains nothing of the kind, so the most expensive bytes in the release still have no failing arm. §4's second-guard paragraph ends: "This release updates both, and §5 test 3's doc assertions are over that sentence and `SKILL.md:145`'s `--status --check` clause". §5 test 3 is "**The two surfaces v0.31.1 exists for.** `tp config --extract` emits the field and `tp validate --project` accepts and rejects it" -- it has no doc assertion. Measured over the whole of §5 (lines 268-311): the substrings `SKILL`, `REFERENCE`, `docs_contract` and even `doc` occur zero times, so none of the eleven tests reaches `skills/tp/` at all. Two consequences. (1) The release changes at least four documented claims and no test forces any of them: the literal pinned at `docs_contract_test.go:96` (verified present as a `const`, and verified live in `SKILL.md`); the `--status --check` clause; `SKILL.md:152-153`'s "tp has no audit-side equivalent of `review_converge_on` yet", which shipping the field falsifies and which this spec still names nowhere; and the two five-name escalation tables §2 itself counts, `REFERENCE.md:347` and `SKILL.md:247` (both verified rendering exactly `skip-gate, raise-review-cap, raise-audit-cap, import-force, other`), which test 10 does not reach because it asserts the refusal's recorded decision, not the tables an agent reads. (2) The citation is off and hides that the two "claims" are one line: `SKILL.md:145` is the `--resolve` step; both the `docs_contract` literal and the `--status --check` clause sit together in the single sentence at `SKILL.md:149`. A stale sentence in `skills/tp/` is one wrong decision per agent per session -- the only cost in this release that recurs without bound -- and it is the one surface the spec leaves unasserted.
suggestion: Give §5 a doc test of its own rather than annexing test 3: assert that `SKILL.md:149`'s sentence no longer claims audit convergence counts every non-`PASS` row unconditionally, that `SKILL.md:152-153` stops saying no audit equivalent exists while still saying the role-scoping divergence is open (Non-Goal 1), and that `REFERENCE.md:347` and `SKILL.md:247` both render six decision names. Its killing mutation is the shipped `docs_contract_test.go:96` literal left in place. Then correct §4's citation from `SKILL.md:145` to `SKILL.md:149` and say the two claims are one sentence.

finding: §4 closes with an exhaustiveness claim over documentation — 'the two sentences this release actually falsifies' — and SKILL.md carries at least two more that blocking makes untrue, neither guarded by any test, so an implementer who works §4's list ships documentation contradicting the feature and nothing reddens. (1) SKILL.md:144, Workflow D step 3: 'a row counts as a finding when status is absent or != PASS; a clean round has zero findings.' Under blocking the second half is flatly false — that is the release's whole content — and this is the sentence a driver agent reads to learn what a clean audit round is. (2) SKILL.md:371: 'An implementation audit always runs to the full 2 consecutive clean rounds and is never cut short by an early cap ... never ship with them open. Implementation correctness is not negotiable.' Under blocking, shipping with warning and info rows open is precisely the sanctioned outcome, so the paragraph forbids the behaviour §2 sells. Neither line is pinned by docs_contract_test.go, so both are silent. By contrast the two §4 does name are the guarded ones — which is the tell: the section enumerated what a test would catch, not what the release falsifies.
suggestion: Replace the count with a list and extend it: SKILL.md:144's clean-round clause, SKILL.md:371's audit-convergence paragraph, SKILL.md:149's divergence clause (docs_contract_test.go:96) and REFERENCE.md's DivergenceHint quote. Or state the scope negatively — 'the release rewords every SKILL.md and REFERENCE.md sentence that asserts audit convergence counts every non-PASS row; the two carrying guards are named because their guards move with them' — which is a rule an implementer can apply to sentences nobody enumerated, rather than a number that goes stale the moment one is missed.

finding: Re-check of test 8's !StateStale barrier, requested for this round. The barrier is REAL but CONDITIONAL, and the current wording does not choose the condition. Facts: engine.Converged = ConsecutiveClean(rounds) >= n && !StateStale(rounds, currentHash) (engine/reviewstate.go:509-511); audit --record (audit_record.go:95) and --status/--check (audit_record.go:333, exit at :401) both go through it with the LIVE hash of the spec argument; and clean is stamped once at record time (audit_record.go:71, clean := findings == 0), so nothing on the audit path ever re-grades a stored round. Two constructions satisfy test 8's words and give different answers. (1) Replay by RE-RECORDING: write each round's copied rows to a file and run `tp audit <fixture-spec> --record` nine and thirteen times. Each record stamps spec_hash from the fixture spec, StateStale is false, and the pinned answers are reachable -- I confirmed the arithmetic against the corpus: blocking 3 / all 9 for v0.35.0 and blocking 3 / all never for v0.36.0 at audit_clean_rounds 2, and 2 and 8 at 1, exactly as §2.1 and test 8 state. (2) Replay by SYNTHESISING round entries -- load the rows, compute clean per policy, build []ReviewRound, call Converged prefix-wise -- where StateStale compares the last synthesised entry's SpecHash against whatever hash the test passes; unless the author deliberately makes them equal, Converged is false for every prefix and 3 and 9 are unreachable, and the natural 'fix' is to assert ConsecutiveClean instead, which silently drops the staleness half of convergence out of the test's coverage. Test 8 says only 'the rows ... copied into testdata/ ... reproduce §2.1's table' and names no fixture spec, no command, and no function. Worse, the two constructions are not free choices: (1) is only available if audit_converge_on is evaluated at RECORD time and (2) only if it is evaluated LIVE, and that is the decision §2 has not made (§2.2's paragraph appears to make it and is refuted by the twin -- see my §2.2 row). Verdict: as written, test 8 does not reach its numbers; it reaches them under one of two constructions the release has not chosen between.
suggestion: Pin the construction. State the command form and the fixture: e.g. 'a temp-dir fixture spec whose bytes do not change across the replay, the rows of each recorded round fed to `tp audit spec.md --record round-N.ndjson` in order, asserting the round at which the emitted converged first becomes true'. Then state that spec_hash is stamped per record so stale stays false, and add the negative arm -- touching the fixture spec after the last record makes converged false -- so the staleness half is covered rather than accidentally excluded. This is unwritable until §2 states record-time vs live evaluation.

finding: Test 10 asserts an observable tp does not produce, and tests 9 and 10 together leave the refusal's only real observable unpinned. Test 10 reads 'A fenced refusal RECORDS --decision audit-converge-on, not other'. A fenced refusal records nothing: refuseUnattended (internal/cli/unattended.go:33-38) and refuseUnattendedCommandField (:44-49) print an output.Error whose HINT is the string 'escalate instead: tp escalate --decision <name> --evidence <what you found>' and exit 2. The only writer of an escalation record is `tp escalate` itself (engine/escalation.go, cli/escalate.go), which the unit runs afterwards. So one engineer asserts the refusal's hint text contains audit-converge-on (passes against a correct implementation) and another asserts a $TP_RUN_DIR/$TP_UNIT_SEQ-escalation.json appears carrying decision: audit-converge-on (fails against every correct implementation). Second half: §2's own code sketch tells the implementer to copy the guard `if engine.Unattended() && engine.FencedCommandField(field) { refuseUnattendedCommandField(field)` at set.go:361-362 and set_project.go:46-47. An implementer who reuses refuseUnattendedCommandField for the third predicate ships the message 'audit_converge_on names a command the driver executes and cannot be set under TP_UNATTENDED, at any layer' -- false, the field names no command -- and BOTH test 9 (exit 2 on each path) and test 10 (the decision name in the hint) still pass, because neither pins the message. §2's whole argument for the enum entry is that 'the reason [is] recoverable only from free text', i.e. it is about message quality, and no test in §5 asserts any of it.
suggestion: Rewrite test 10 as 'a fenced refusal exits 2 and its hint names `tp escalate --decision audit-converge-on`, not `other`' -- the observable tp actually emits -- and add to test 9 an assertion on the refusal MESSAGE, pinning that it names audit_converge_on as a convergence policy and not as a command the driver executes, so reusing refuseUnattendedCommandField goes red.

finding: cdcc3cc added a provenance note to spec/0.46.0.md §8.4: "§2–§8.3 come from v0.36.0's audit; this comes from v0.37.0's review." The boundary is drawn in the wrong place and the repair therefore introduced a fresh false claim while fixing an unstated one. §8.1, §8.2 and §8.3 were written in commit 43f29e8 (2026-09-02 01:11), thirty-four minutes before cdcc3cc, and that commit's own message says why: "Measured in round 4: spec/0.46.0.md contained zero occurrences of severity, wontfix, disposition, --resolve or dedupAuditRows" — i.e. they came from v0.37.0's review, exactly like §8.4. Move the note out of §8.4 to the file header or §1, since it now qualifies §1's claim rather than one subsection's.

finding: Bumping the manifest to 0.37.0 during review round 6 sets the SessionStart preflight's minimum to a version that has no released binary, and the effect is live rather than theoretical. Measured: /tmp/tp-dev/tp built from this tree reports v0.36.1-0.20260901224505-8dc02b58bd44+dirty, and running hooks/session-start.sh against it exits 2 with "tp v0.36.1-... is older than the tp plugin's minimum 0.37.0", so tp resume --compact is no longer injected into any Claude Code session in this repository for the rest of the cycle — the plugin's own orientation, during the cycle that dogfoods it. The remedy the hook prints cannot fix it: go install ...@latest resolves to v0.36.0. hooks/session-start.sh:44-49 documents refusing the pre-tag window as correct, so this is not the hook misbehaving; what changed is the window's length. CLAUDE.md:164's rule is "bump → commit → tag (the >= comparison exists so that window is legal)", which assumes a window measured in one commit, and marketplace.json's source is "./", so anyone who runs claude plugin update tp@tp before the tag gets a manifest demanding a binary that does not exist.
suggestion: Either move the bump back to immediately before the tag and let TestPluginVersionIsBumpedWhenPluginContentChanges hold against the version at the last tag rather than forcing a bump mid-cycle, or state explicitly in CLAUDE.md:164 that a mid-cycle bump disables the plugin's orientation for the remainder of the cycle and that the hook's install hint is unfollowable in that window.

finding: 8dc02b5 replaced the pluginMinVersion constant with a helper that reads .claude-plugin/plugin.json, which is right for the four call sites in hooks_session_start_test.go but turned one assertion into a tautology. TestPluginManifestDeclaresIdentity:92 now reads assert.GreaterOrEqual(t, comparePluginVersions(t, manifest.Version, pluginMinVersion(t)), 0): manifest.Version comes from readRepoDoc(t, pluginManifestPath) and pluginMinVersion(t) reads filepath.Join(repoRoot(t), pluginManifestPath) — the same field of the same file, so comparePluginVersions always returns 0 and the assertion cannot fail for any manifest content. finding: The file header records the rewrite decision this file was rebuilt on: the withdrawn-draft prose "had grown to 77 of the file's 306 lines, which is spec/0.43.0.md §2's repair-verbosity class measured on this file." finding: The file's header records deleting this exact class -- "The prose recording which drafts were withdrawn is gone with them: it had grown to 77 of the file's 306 lines" -- and the deletion is now fully undone. Counting the spans whose subject is a withdrawn draft, a corrected count, or which round changed what: §1:22-25 (4), §2:34-46 (13), §2:67-68 (2), §2:132-133 (2), §2.2:169-175 (7), §3:177-205 (29), §4:225-229 (5), §4:239-243 (5), §4:255-258 (4), §4:265-266 (2), §5:270-276 (7) -- **80 of 312 lines, 26%**, against the header's deleted 77 of 306. Four of those eleven spans were written or extended this round, in §1, §2, §2.2 and §4. §2's span is the one that states the case against itself: "it is recorded here as provenance, not as scope, because a scope sentence already satisfied cannot fail as acceptance." That is the correct test and it disqualifies the thirteen lines that follow it -- an implementer reading §2's opening paragraph for what to build gets one buildable sentence (the field, two values, task override > project config > built-in, the hint machinery) and then twelve lines on a sweep already done, which two shipped specs keep a wrong copy that must not be edited, that `TP_RUNNER_SEAM` and `notify_cmd` are exceptions to a precedence rule this field does not use, and a note about how to scope a grep so it does not match the sentence doing the scoping. suggestion: Apply the section's own test to the section: keep a provenance sentence only where a reader who did not read it would make the mistake again, and move the rest to the round files, which already hold it. Concretely -- §2's opening paragraph reduces to the field, its two values, its precedence and its hint, plus the one sentence that stops the five-layer chain being re-copied; §1's "This paragraph described the two-deliverable release for one round after the cut" goes (the paragraph is now correct, and the Overview is the highest-traffic text in the file); §2.2, §4's four parenthetical corrections and §5's preamble each keep their result and drop which draft was wrong. §3 was filed separately in round 6.

finding: The repaired fence points at the right shape and the code block it prints ships a false message, with no test in §5 that can catch it. §2 says 'What to copy instead is the string-shaped fence that ships today' and reproduces `if engine.Unattended() && engine.FencedCommandField(field) { refuseUnattendedCommandField(field)`, then says 'So the work is a third predicate beside FencedCapField and FencedCommandField, and that guard copied at both sites.' A third PREDICATE plus that refusal function is not enough: refuseUnattendedCommandField (unattended.go:44-49) emits the literal '%s names a command the driver executes and cannot be set under TP_UNATTENDED, at any layer', which is untrue of a convergence policy field, and its hint is built from escalationDecision(field) — so the two edits §2 does name (predicate, enum entry) leave an implementation that exits 2, escalates as audit-converge-on, and tells the operator that audit_converge_on is a command the driver executes. §5 test 9 asserts exit codes only and test 10 asserts the decision name only, so both pass. The work is three things, not two: a predicate, a refusal function with its own message, and the enum entry. Verified in the tree: set.go:361-364 and set_project.go:46-49 are exactly where the snippet says, so the placement half of the repair is correct.
suggestion: Name the third piece and one assertion that pins it: 'a refuseUnattendedPolicyField(field) beside refuseUnattendedCommandField, whose message says the field is a convergence policy and a user-approved decision rather than a command the driver executes', and extend test 9 to assert the refusal text does not claim the field names a command — killing input, a verbatim reuse of refuseUnattendedCommandField.

finding: §2 pins the precedence — 'task override > project config > built-in' — and names none of the three sites that make the project-config layer actually carry the field, one of which fails silently and is caught by no test the release proposes. (1) engine/projectconfig.go:85-94, knownWorkflowKeys: a key absent from that map is reported as 'unknown workflow key' and dropped, so .tp/config.json carrying audit_converge_on would resolve to the built-in all while tp reports a warning nobody reads. (2) parseWorkflowOverride needs a string case beside review_converge_on's at :141-150, whose comment records the decision this release must repeat: not validated at parse time, surfaced raw by tp config --resolved, rejected only by a consuming command. (3) model.WorkflowOverride.IsEmpty (model/projectconfig.go:87-103) enumerates all sixteen fields by hand; a seventeenth left out makes (&WorkflowOverride{AuditConvergeOn: ptr("blocking")}).IsEmpty() return true. That is the silent one: IsEmpty has no production caller in the tree today (measured — the only non-test references are its own definition), so no test in §5 and none in the existing suite would redden, and the wrong answer sits latent until the first caller. runfields_test.go:194-204 shows the shape of the guard the repository already uses for exactly this. Sites (1) and (2) are at least reachable by §5 test 2 IF that test resolves through a real .tp/config.json rather than a hand-built struct — which §5 does not say either.

And make §5 test 2 resolve the project layer through a written .tp/config.json, so (1) and (2) have a failing arm; add an IsEmpty assertion beside runfields_test.go:194-204's for (3).

finding: §2 says the field is "rejected with the same hint machinery when the value is neither" and §5 test 2 says "an invalid value is refused with the same hint shape review_converge_on uses". Neither names an exit code, and the twin they point at deliberately uses two different ones on two different paths: a bad literal argument is a USAGE error, exit 2 (set.go:376, set_project.go:69, both with engine.ReviewConvergeOnHint), while a stored value that fails to resolve at a consuming command is a VALIDATION error, exit 1 -- a distinction with its own shipped test, TestReviewConvergeOn_InvalidStoredExitsOne, and its own code comment at reviewconvergeon.go:12-15. "The same hint shape" pins the hint string and says nothing about which of the two paths the audit twin gets. The consuming surface is unnamed too: for review it is any command that resolves the field, for audit it would have to be tp audit --record/--status, and §2 never says so. Under this spec an implementation can ship write-time validation only, leave a hand-edited .tp/config.json value unvalidated at the audit sink, and satisfy §5 test 2 -- which is the failure mode tp's own exit-code table exists to prevent.
suggestion: State both arms in §2: exit 2 at the two set surfaces for a literal argument, exit 1 with the same hint at tp audit --record/--status for a stored value that is neither `all` nor `blocking`. Give §5 test 2 a second killing mutation for the stored-value arm (a resolver that trusts a stored value it did not validate).

finding: §2's escalation paragraph makes a counted claim — 'the enum's cardinality is asserted in nine places that must move with it, counted' — and the count is short by at least one, in the file the release must edit anyway. skills/tp/SKILL.md:372 spells the closed set out literally: `tp escalate --decision <skip-gate|raise-review-cap|raise-audit-cap|import-force|other>`. It is a second SKILL.md site, distinct from the :247 inventory row the nine include, and it is a driver-facing instruction: left alone it tells every unit under tp run that audit-converge-on is not a legal decision, which is precisely the escalation §2 adds the enum entry to make possible. A second, smaller point about the same list: of the nine, only cli/escalate_test.go:158's five-literal loop actually fails when a sixth value is added; engine/escalation.go:14,29,39,47, engine/escalation_test.go:60 (a subtest NAME) and fakerunner main.go:260 (a comment; the record's value at :263 is 'invent-one', chosen to be outside the set and still outside it at six) are prose that goes stale silently. So the paragraph both undercounts the sites and overstates what 'asserted' buys — a reader budgeting from it expects nine failing tests and gets one.
suggestion: Add SKILL.md:372 to the list, and split it in two so the budget is honest: 'one assertion fails when the set grows — cli/escalate_test.go:158's five-literal loop; the rest are prose and doc tables that must be swept because nothing will fail if they are not: engine/escalation.go's four comments, engine/escalation_test.go:60's subtest name, fakerunner main.go:260's comment, escalate.go:41's help text, REFERENCE.md:347, SKILL.md:247 and SKILL.md:372.' A count bound to a grep (the literal `import-force, other`) would not have gone stale here.

finding: §2.2 is a numbered subsection, 16 lines, whose second half establishes that its own subject does not exist for this release: "those 67 rows are read by no predicate this release adds", the live risk is forward-looking instead, "across v0.33.0-v0.36.0 there are **zero** out-of-enum severities in 238 non-`PASS` rows", and test 7 uses a legacy row "because it is convenient and real, not because the case is live". Its whole operative content is one clause already entailed by §2's fail-closed rule: legacy rows count as blocking, so no migration, no rewrite, no sink validation. A heading is not free prose in tp, and this is measurable rather than stylistic: `tp review` renders the section outline into every role prompt -- my own round-7 prompt lists "2.2 The 67 legacy rows" as a focus item and instructs me to apply my lens to it -- so an inert subsection is bought into five prompts per round for every remaining round, and each role spends its attention discovering there is nothing there. The same signal reaches the decomposer, which reads headings to size the task list and finds a named population of 67 rows in fifteen round files with no task attached to it, and reaches `--diff-from`, which reports §2.2 as a changed section when only its null result was reworded (it was reported MODIFIED to me this round while its line count did not change). The section is also the only place §2's own justification is restated in a second, different form -- §2 grounds the fail-closed rule on v0.31.0 §4.1, §2.2 re-grounds it on a forward-looking corpus argument -- so a reader who takes §2.2 as the reason gets a reason the release does not depend on.
suggestion: Delete the subsection and put its result in §2 beside the fail-closed rule as one sentence: "Sixty-seven non-`PASS` rows recorded across v0.29.0-v0.32.0 carry `high`/`medium`/`low`; the fail-closed rule counts them as blocking, so nothing migrates and nothing is validated at the sink -- and they are not why the rule exists, since `ReviewRound.Clean` is stamped at record time and no predicate this release adds reads them." Keep the corpus counts where they are load-bearing -- test 7's note that all 67 carry a present, non-null severity, which is why it needs three fixtures.

finding: Non-Goal 6 now reads "... The review side emits `nonblocking_open` (`review_record.go:231`) Four places pin its absence on `--record`/`--status` by name, counted: ...". finding: The reversed-guard paragraph makes a deliberately precise dependency claim -- "only :490 needs §2's fail-closed rule to hold, because signalRow (audit_signal_test.go:40-42) emits no severity key. :493-:500 read a payload recorded before the reversed line and are unaffected" -- and skips the assertions between them. Reading the function (469-503): after the reversal at 472-474 the tp set call succeeds and writes audit_converge_on=blocking into the project config for the remainder of the test, and lines 483-487 then re-record a round and assert on that new payload's role_streaks. Those two assertions are the only ones executed against a payload recorded AFTER the reversed line, which is exactly the position the paragraph's own reasoning says matters, and they are named in neither the dependent set nor the unaffected set. (They do in fact survive, because §2 scopes blocking to `clean` and leaves auditRoundOpenByRole reading AuditRowIsPass alone -- but that is the argument the paragraph makes for :493-:500 and declines to make here.) The same omission leaves the test's own comment block at 454-468 -- "There is no audit_converge_on knob to flip" -- unmentioned, though it is falsified by the same two lines.
suggestion: Extend the enumeration to all eleven assertions, or state the rule once instead of listing exceptions: every assertion after the reversed line runs under audit_converge_on=blocking; :490 depends on §2's fail-closed rule because signalRow carries no severity; :485-487 depend on §2's boundary that blocking governs `clean` and not role_streaks. Add the comment block at 454-468 to the docs/test text this release must update.

finding: 8dc02b5 also re-encoded the author name in the manifest, from "Yunus Emre Deligöz" to "Yunus Emre Delig\u00f6z", which its commit message does not mention — the message is about deriving the preflight minimum and bumping the version. finding: CLAUDE.md's roadmap table carries a Lines column that this batch invalidated for the two files it touched, and CLAUDE.md:230-236 makes that column load-bearing — it is the measured predictor the thirteen-release split was decided on. finding: §1's repair left a sentence that narrates §1's own past state inside the paragraph an implementer derives scope from: 'This paragraph described the two-deliverable release for one round after the cut, which is the shape of defect §3 exists to stop the next reader re-proposing.'
